title: War and peace
subtitle: sanctions, escalate, ceasefire, wage war on
summary: Describe conflict accurately - from diplomacy and sanctions to civil unrest, escalation and ceasefires - and use the metaphors of warfare in everyday English.

lesson.heading: When diplomacy fails
lesson.text: War is often seen as a **last resort** - something you do when everything else has failed - when relations break down and **diplomacy** and **economic sanctions** have failed. Sanctions are official orders, such as the stopping of trade, taken against a country to make it obey international law.

examples.text: When **diplomacy** and economic **sanctions** had failed, the Cabinet voted to take military action.
War should always be a **last resort** when all other avenues have been explored.

lesson.note: Diplomacy covers the activities concerning the relationships between governments.

lesson.heading: Military action and its cost
lesson.text: Even the best-planned operations, carried out with the latest hi-tech **weaponry**, result in **civilian casualties** - people injured or killed who are not members of the military or the police. **Military intervention** may aim at **regime change**, but the leaders of **tyrannical** regimes are the hardest to **overthrow**.

examples.text: The armed forces moved a large amount of **weaponry** to the battlefront.
There were many civilian **casualties** as a result of the bombing raid.
The war brought about **regime** change. The former dictator was **overthrown** and forced to flee.
The **intervention** of the United Nations helped to restore peace.

lesson.heading: Civil war
lesson.text: Civil war - war between groups who live in the same country - often begins with **civil unrest** and **clashes** between **rival** **ethnic**, religious or political groups. It may **escalate** into **all-out** war and end in the brutal **suppression** of one group by another, or in **ethnic cleansing** and **massacres**.

examples.text: Occasional violence between the two groups eventually **escalated** into **all-out** civil war.
There were violent **clashes** between police and demonstrators in the capital city.
The government forces were accused of carrying out ethnic **cleansing**.
During the war, a **massacre** occurred in a village near the border.

lesson.note: Ethnic means national or racial; rival groups compete against one another.

lesson.heading: After the fighting
lesson.text: **Conflict resolution** - finding a way to end conflict and the negative feelings between groups - may take years to bring into effect, and **mistrust** and **hatred** between groups in the same country may continue long afterwards.

examples.text: The process of conflict **resolution** was successful and the country has now been at peace for ten years.
There had been a longstanding **mistrust** between the two tribes.
Irrational **hatred** of people of other ethnic groups is one of the root causes of conflict.
The general was a **brutal** dictator who ruled for 18 years.

lesson.heading: Words for acts of war
rows: attack by surrounding a place for a period of time
an agreement during a war to stop fighting for a time
an agreement between two armies or groups to stop fighting
a planned group of military activities
the fight of people against their own government

lesson.heading: Keeping and watching the peace
lesson.text: A **peacekeeping force** is made up of neutral soldiers who keep the peace in a divided society, and international **observers** are an outside, neutral body who monitor events. A **suicide bomber** lets off explosives, deliberately killing themselves in the process.

examples.text: The UN sent in a **peacekeeping** force to keep the two sides in the civil war apart.
International **observers** monitored the election and concluded that it had been fair.
A **suicide** bomber disguised as a police officer killed 15 people in an attack today.
Hostilities finally **ceased** after five years of **bloodshed**.

lesson.heading: Metaphors of warfare
lesson.text: War vocabulary is often used metaphorically in everyday English: you **wage war on** a social problem, journalists **besiege** a house, companies run an advertising **campaign** or **battle** for market supremacy, and you can have a **fight on your hands**.

examples.text: The government is **waging war on** drink-driving.
Paparazzi are **besieging** the star's Hollywood home.
A major advertising **campaign** was planned to launch the new cosmetics range.
We have a major **fight on our hands** if we are to save the company from bankruptcy.

lesson.note: A fleet normally consists of a large number of ships, but we also say a fleet of cars.

lesson.text: A truce is temporary, agreed so that talks can begin; a ceasefire is the formal agreement to stop fighting.

exercises.prompt: War should always be a last ___ when all other avenues have been explored.
exercises.hint: (what you do when everything else has failed)
exercises.explanation: A last resort is something you do when everything else has failed.

exercises.prompt: There were many civilian ___ as a result of the bombing raid.
exercises.explanation: Civilian casualties are people injured or killed who are not in the military or police.

exercises.prompt: There were violent ___ between police and demonstrators in the capital city.
exercises.explanation: Clashes are fights or arguments between rival groups.

exercises.prompt: Occasional violence between the two groups eventually ___ into all-out civil war.
exercises.explanation: To escalate is to become greater or more serious.

exercises.prompt: The UN sent in a ___ force to keep the two sides in the civil war apart.
exercises.explanation: A peacekeeping force is made up of neutral soldiers who keep the peace in a divided society.

exercises.prompt: A convoy of lorries was ___ by enemy soldiers in a remote valley yesterday.
exercises.explanation: To ambush is to attack unexpectedly from secret positions.

exercises.prompt: The ___ of the city lasted six months before the enemy troops were pushed back.
exercises.explanation: A siege is the surrounding of a place for a period of time in order to attack it.

exercises.prompt: The government has ___ war on the drug cartels for the last ten years.
exercises.explanation: To wage war on something is to fight a war against it, here used metaphorically.

exercises.prompt: The former dictator was ___ and forced to flee from the country.
exercises.explanation: To overthrow someone is to remove them from power using force.

exercises.prompt: After a year of fighting, the two sides agreed to a ___ to enable peace negotiations to start.
exercises.explanation: A truce (or a ceasefire) is an agreement to stop fighting; here it allows talks to begin.

exercises.prompt: Official orders such as the stopping of trade, taken against a country to make it obey international law, are called ___.
exercises.explanation: Economic sanctions are used as an alternative to military action.

exercises.statement: The intervention of the United Nations in the situation helped to restore peace.
exercises.explanation: Correct - intervention is intentionally becoming involved in a difficult situation to improve it.

exercises.statement: A rebellion is a fight between two different countries.
exercises.explanation: A rebellion is a fight by people against their own government; rebels fight the dictatorship.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression describe fighting, or stopping the fighting?
Put this sentence about civil war in order.
exercises.answer: Civil war often begins with civil unrest and clashes between rival groups
exercises.explanation: Civil unrest is disagreement or fighting between groups within one country.
